title: Sexual Assault Is a Free Speech Issue
gist: WIRED's Ej Dickson interviews law professor and Cyber Civil Rights Initiative president Mary Anne Franks about the online doxing of the anonymous Jane Doe who accused seven Cornell Chi Phi members of assault. Franks argues that sexual abuse is itself a free-speech issue because it silences victims. She says the 'Elon Muskification' of free-speech rhetoric and X's lax enforcement have removed the disincentives against mob doxing, and that today's social platforms cannot safely carry accusations like this.

themes.theme: Sexual abuse reframed as a speech harm

insights.claim: Mary Anne Franks argues that sexual abuse is a free-speech issue. In her view it silences victims, who drop out of classes, journalism or politics, so tolerating abuse amounts to deciding that women's speech does not matter.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: This reframing can be used to push back on platform 'free speech' arguments against regulating image-based abuse and doxing.
insights.quote: sexual abuse is a free speech issue. It silences people
insights.locator: Part of what we’ve tried to say

insights.claim: Franks says the 'cultural fetishization' of an abstract idea of free speech takes the body out of the debate, so physical safety ends up framed as the opposite of speech.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: Free-speech framing is the main rhetorical defense that platforms and doxers use against safety rules.
insights.quote: Somehow physical safety becomes oppositional to this supreme value of speech.
insights.locator: When you have a cultural fetishization

insights.claim: Franks notes that private universities such as Cornell are not bound by the First Amendment. She adds that even public universities can still enforce anti-harassment discipline, so claims that punishing misogynistic speech on campus violates the First Amendment are legally false.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: This makes it easier legally for universities to discipline students over online harassment, whatever the backlash.
insights.quote: private universities are not bound by the First Amendment
insights.locator: I think that the more things change

insights.claim: Franks says tech platforms opposed criminalizing deepfakes on free-speech grounds. Women's bodily autonomy is repeatedly the thing that gets traded away in those arguments.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: Deepfake and NCII legislation will keep running into platform free-speech lobbying, which is a regulatory risk to watch.
insights.locator: It also reminds me of the conversation about deepfakes

insights.claim: Franks describes an 'Elon Muskification' of free speech: Musk's promise to bring free speech back to Twitter gave many people permission to dress up misogynistic or racist conduct as free-speech activism and expect to be praised for it.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: Brand-safety and regulatory pressure on X stays high while its moderation is seen as permitting harassment.
insights.quote: it is kind of the Elon Muskification of the free speech argument
insights.locator: It’s hard to know where to start

insights.claim: Dickson observed that tweets doxing the woman believed to be Jane Doe were not taken down and mostly did not get notes, despite X's policy against doxing. Franks says the loudest free-speech defenders shield speech they approve of and suppress speech they do not.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: This is evidence of a gap between X's stated policy and its enforcement, which matters for its exposure under the EU DSA and other online-safety regimes.
insights.locator: One of the things I was really struck by

insights.claim: Franks argues that because Musk has an enormous megaphone and says openly that he got Donald Trump elected, his redefinition of free speech signals to the whole world that misogyny and racism are acceptable.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: The concentration of platform ownership and political power makes moderation policy a political issue.
insights.locator: This is someone who quite candidly

themes.theme: Mob doxing and the end of disincentives

insights.claim: Franks says doxing a victim used to carry a social cost, but now people who do it under their own names are validated, given attention and even praised. That reversal of incentives is what she sees as new.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: Platform algorithms that reward pile-ons structurally amplify harassment, which keeps liability and regulatory risk alive for engagement-driven platforms.
insights.quote: You will get validated. You will get attention.
insights.locator: We really seem to have removed

insights.claim: Franks concludes that social media platforms as they now operate can never support safely releasing names in sexual-assault accusations, because the 'bloodlust' that drives engagement inevitably produces mobs, swatting and the doxing of innocent people who share a name.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: Pressure may build for victim-anonymity laws and for platform duty-of-care rules.
insights.quote: The kind of bloodlust that is the currency of social media platforms, it’s incompatible with releasing information like this.
insights.locator: You want people to be held accountable

insights.claim: Dickson describes the 'burnerverse' as a community of anonymous college-sports fan accounts, many run by fraternity members, that dox young women for sport. These accounts amplified a University of Florida student's nonconsensual intimate video on X along with her full name and sorority.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: Anonymous burner networks on X are a channel for NCII spread that platforms are not containing.
insights.locator: Last month, I published an investigation into the burnerverse

themes.theme: Apps as amplifiers of fraternity culture

insights.claim: According to Jane Doe's lawsuit, one of the alleged assailants posted an explicit photo of her to a fraternity Snapchat group to announce that she was available, and that post is how other members knew to enter the room.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: Snapchat could face litigation and reputational exposure as a tool used in coordinating group abuse.

insights.claim: Franks argues that Snapchat succeeded with nude-photo sharing because users believed the images would disappear, and that this sense of ephemerality almost gamifies the behavior.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: Ephemeral-messaging design is increasingly seen as a cause of abuse, which could invite design-code regulation.
insights.quote: It’s this idea that it’s ephemeral somehow, one that almost gamifies what’s happening.
insights.locator: I think that the Snapchat platform

insights.claim: Franks says technology adds performance and spectacle to long-standing male-bonding abuse, which turns the whole internet into 'your online frat' and creates permanent, borderless exposure for victims.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: Permanence and global reach raise the harm, and the damages, attached to NCII incidents.
insights.quote: Now you can turn the entire internet basically into your online frat.
insights.locator: It is now something you can get an even larger audience

insights.claim: Franks reports that sextortion schemes are increasingly victimizing young men, including young teenagers, which she calls an 'epidemic' that often starts from loneliness and a desire for connection.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: Teen-safety features and age-assurance regulation are a growing compliance area for platforms that serve minors.
insights.quote: we’ve actually seen a lot more victimization of young men when it comes to sextortion schemes
insights.locator: We do have a lot of conversations about image-based

insights.claim: Franks argues that platforms which tell users they deserve attention and that attention can be gamed will make things worse for everyone, and especially for vulnerable people. She recommends deliberately using social media less.
insights.speaker: Ej Dickson
insights.so_what: This is part of the cultural backlash against attention-economy business models that could weigh on engagement over time.
insights.locator: That’s a really terrible thing to do to humanity
